title: Arcadia Health x Redwood Inference — Discovery (Private/VPC requirements)
next_steps: Redwood to send Arcadia the Private (VPC) deployment overview + security packet (SOC 2, data handling, logging controls).
Arcadia to confirm preferred cloud/region and whether VPC endpoint / PrivateLink is required.
Schedule 60-min technical deep dive (networking, KMS/key ownership, audit log schema/export, retention controls).
Arcadia to share current baseline metrics (p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, error rates) and traffic shape for a potential pilot.
Align on design partner success criteria and internal approval path for participating in case study/reference program (may be anonymized).
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: May 6, 2025
Time: 2:02pm PT
Duration: 48 min
Platform: Zoom (Fireflies)

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference) — AE
- Simran Kaur (Redwood Inference) — Solutions Architect
- Maya Patel (Arcadia Health) — Director, Platform Engineering
- Chris Reynolds (Arcadia Health) — Staff Security Engineer
- Elena Torres (Arcadia Health) — Principal ML Engineer

Summary (auto-generated)
Arcadia Health shared that their LLM workloads handle regulated healthcare data and require VPC/private networking, strong audit logging, and strict retention controls. They described their current inference approach (mixed vendor APIs + early self-hosting), and what would make Redwood a viable design partner: private deployment option, key ownership/KMS, configurable logs, reproducible performance metrics, and a clear security review path.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Current LLM use cases and traffic
- VPC / private networking constraints
- Audit logs and retention requirements
- Current stack and pain points
- Success criteria for a pilot + design partner program

Action Items (auto-generated)
- Avery: Send Arcadia a one-pager on Redwood Private (VPC) + example network diagram by EOW.
- Simran: Propose a metrics/benchmarking plan (latency + cost) and list required inputs by Thursday.
- Chris (Arcadia): Provide Arcadia’s logging/retention policy summary and preferred audit log format (JSON/CSV) by next week.
- Maya (Arcadia): Identify internal approvers for a potential reference program (security + comms) and confirm if anonymized is acceptable.

Transcript

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. I know we grabbed 45, we can end early if we’re done. Um, goal today is just discovery—understand what you’re building, constraints, and see if a Private/VPC deployment makes sense. And then we can line up a deeper technical session with Simran.

[00:18] Maya Patel: Sounds good.

[00:19] Elena Torres: Yep.

[00:20] Chris Reynolds: Works.

[00:22] Avery Johnson: Great. Maybe quick intros—Maya you want to start?

[00:26] Maya Patel: Sure. I run platform engineering. We own our internal developer platform, Kubernetes, networking, and compliance controls. We’re the team that gets pulled in when, like, “hey can we run this model with PHI?”

[00:41] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[00:42] Maya Patel: Elena is ML engineering, and Chris is security engineering. We’re evaluating an inference layer for a couple product groups.

[00:52] Avery Johnson: Perfect. I’m Avery, I cover healthcare and regulated accounts here. Simran is our solutions architect, she’ll do most of the technical grilling.

[01:02] Simran Kaur: Hi everyone.

[01:04] Elena Torres: Hi.

[01:05] Avery Johnson: Cool. Elena—can you give the 60-second of the use case? What’s the user-facing thing?

[01:12] Elena Torres: Yeah. So, there’s two. One is clinician note summarization inside our care management app. The other is member message triage—like classifying inbound messages, drafting suggested replies. Both are… they touch PHI, so we’ve been very conservative.

[01:33] Avery Johnson: Got it. Is it primarily chat completions style, or embeddings too?

[01:37] Elena Torres: Both. Summarization is generation. The triage is embeddings plus reranking, and then generation for draft.

[01:47] Simran Kaur: What’s the traffic profile, roughly? Like QPS, peak vs average, and response length.

[01:54] Elena Torres: Uh, today it’s small because we’ve limited it. Maybe 2 to 5 QPS peak in pilots. But if we roll out it’s, I don’t know, 50 QPS bursts in business hours. Response length—summaries can be 200 to 600 tokens. Draft replies similar.

[02:13] Simran Kaur: Okay. And the input context—are you passing long notes, like thousands of tokens?

[02:18] Elena Torres: Yes. That’s part of why we’re calling. The note can be, like, 6 to 12 pages. We chunk it, but still large. We also have some templates.

[02:30] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. And current stack—how are you doing it now?

[02:34] Elena Torres: It’s a mix. For non-PHI experiments, we used OpenAI and sometimes Anthropic. For PHI, we tried Azure OpenAI with a private endpoint, but we got stuck in procurement and policy questions. And we’re also testing self-hosted vLLM on EKS with a couple open models.

[02:56] Maya Patel: To be clear, we don’t want “random traffic to the internet.” It has to be private networking. And we need audit logs.

[03:05] Avery Johnson: Yep, understood. When you say VPC—are you thinking fully private control plane in your VPC, or like a hosted service accessible via PrivateLink?

[03:16] Maya Patel: PrivateLink is acceptable if it’s truly private and we can lock egress. But we need to understand where any metadata goes, and what’s logged.

[03:27] Chris Reynolds: And key ownership. We’re pushing for customer-managed keys. If you encrypt at rest with your KMS, that’s a harder sell.

[03:35] Simran Kaur: That’s helpful. Redwood has a “Private” deployment mode where the data plane can sit in your VPC with customer-managed networking, and we can integrate with your KMS. But we’ll want to walk through specifics because it depends on cloud and the architecture.

[03:52] Avery Johnson: Before we go too deep, can we just capture top constraints? Maya, Chris, what are the “non-negotiables”?

[04:00] Maya Patel: Okay. Non-negotiables: VPC networking. No training on our data. No retention of prompts/responses beyond what’s needed for operational logs—and ideally configurable to zero. Audit logs that are exportable. And SSO/RBAC for the console. 

[04:20] Chris Reynolds: Add: we need a BAA. HIPAA. And we need a clear SOC 2 report. Also we need log retention controls: our policy is security logs retained one year, application logs 30 days, but PHI must not land in logs.

[04:36] Simran Kaur: When you say “audit logs,” what events do you need? Like who called what model, request IDs, admin actions, or actual payload logging?

[04:46] Chris Reynolds: Admin actions, auth events, model changes, access to keys, configuration. Request-level metadata is fine—timestamps, token counts, latency. But we cannot have raw prompts/responses stored.

[05:00] Maya Patel: Even “debug mode” needs to be controlled. Like, if someone flips a switch and suddenly we’re storing prompts, that’s a problem.

[05:09] Simran Kaur: Yep. So, we separate operational metrics from content logging, and we can talk about guardrails. Typically we advise customers to keep payload logging off, and rely on token-level metrics and trace IDs.

[05:23] Avery Johnson: Elena, what’s the pain with the current approach? Is it cost, latency, ops overhead, compliance… all of the above?

[05:30] Elena Torres: All of the above. With Azure we couldn’t get a straight answer on retention and whether prompts were used for anything. With self-hosting, it’s just, like, we’re now in the GPU business. Also p95 latency is not stable; we see spikes when batching changes or the node is busy.

[05:51] Simran Kaur: Do you have any numbers, even rough? p50 and p95.

[05:56] Elena Torres: For our EKS test: p50 is maybe 900ms to first token for short prompts, but p95 goes to 4 to 8 seconds when the context is long. And we saw some timeouts. I don’t trust our setup.

[06:13] Simran Kaur: That’s consistent with queueing and KV cache pressure. Also depends on continuous batching parameters.

[06:20] Maya Patel: Sorry—KV cache is…

[06:22] Simran Kaur: It’s the attention cache. Basically for long context, memory usage grows, and you can get thrash if it’s not managed carefully.

[06:30] Maya Patel: Okay.

[06:32] Avery Johnson: Helpful. For design partner—what does that mean to you? Like what outcome would make this a win?

[06:40] Maya Patel: Win is: we can deploy this in a compliant way, and the platform team isn’t paged every week. Also, if we do a pilot, we want reproducible numbers and clear operational tooling.

[06:55] Chris Reynolds: Win is we pass security review without “exceptions.” No special-case approvals.

[07:01] Elena Torres: Win is stable latency and a cost model we can predict. If we have to reserve capacity, fine, but it needs to be understandable.

[07:11] Avery Johnson: Got it. On the latency—do you have an SLO?

[07:15] Elena Torres: For the clinician workflow, we want under 2 seconds to first token and under 8 seconds total for typical notes. For triage, it’s more like under 500ms for embeddings and rerank.

[07:29] Simran Kaur: And concurrency? Like, do you need burst handling or steady.

[07:33] Elena Torres: Bursty around clinic hours. We also have batch jobs overnight.

[07:40] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. Redwood can do hosted, dedicated, and private. For you, I think we’re talking Dedicated or Private. If your requirement is VPC with customer-managed network, that’s Private.

[07:55] Maya Patel: Yeah, we’re leaning that way.

[07:57] Chris Reynolds: We’d still consider “dedicated but hosted” if there’s private connectivity and contractual controls. But likely Private.

[08:06] Simran Kaur: Can I ask about where you’re running today? AWS?

[08:10] Maya Patel: AWS primary. Some Azure for a different business unit, but platform is AWS.

[08:16] Simran Kaur: Okay. So, VPC endpoints are on the table.

[08:20] Avery Johnson: On audit logs, do you need to push into Splunk, Datadog, S3, something?

[08:25] Chris Reynolds: Splunk for security. S3 for raw archive. Ideally we can pull via API or have a push. JSON lines is fine.

[08:33] Simran Kaur: Great. We have audit log exports; I’ll confirm the formats and what’s available in Private.

[08:41] Avery Johnson: And data retention—when you say “no retention,” is it literally zero, or can we retain minimal metadata for troubleshooting?

[08:49] Chris Reynolds: Metadata is okay. Content is not. For content, zero.

[08:55] Maya Patel: We might allow content in a very limited troubleshooting window, but it requires a break-glass process and documented approvals.

[09:04] Simran Kaur: Understood. We can talk about a break-glass workflow conceptually, but we generally try to avoid content logging entirely.

[09:14] Avery Johnson: On the current vendor APIs—do you have any policy issues with sending PHI to OpenAI/Anthropic today?

[09:21] Elena Torres: We do not send PHI. We redact or de-identify for experiments, but it’s imperfect and it hurts quality. That’s why we need a compliant path.

[09:33] Avery Johnson: Makes total sense.

[09:35] Simran Kaur: Another question: do you need regional residency? Like US-only.

[09:40] Chris Reynolds: US-only. And ideally single region. Also we want to prevent data from leaving the VPC.

[09:47] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[09:49] Avery Johnson: Okay. Shifting gears a bit—design partner program. We’re running a structured customer reference program. It’s optional, but if this is a fit and you get value, we’d ask for participation in a case study or reference calls. Does that immediately cause heartburn?

[10:04] Maya Patel: Public case study would be hard. We can maybe do anonymized, or “healthcare provider” style.

[10:11] Chris Reynolds: Also anything public goes through legal and comms, and they’re… slow.

[10:16] Avery Johnson: Yep, totally. We can start with “reference-call only” or anonymized story. We’re not trying to force it.

[10:23] Elena Torres: If it works well, I can imagine a technical talk or something, but it depends.

[10:29] Avery Johnson: Great. For now it’s just helpful to know the approval path. We’ll keep it low-pressure.

[10:36] Simran Kaur: Elena, on the model side—are you set on a particular model family? Open models vs proprietary.

[10:42] Elena Torres: We prefer open models for compliance and cost. We tried Llama variants. We also tested Mistral. Quality is okay but we need consistent throughput. We may use a smaller model for triage.

[10:58] Simran Kaur: Okay. Redwood supports a catalog, and for Private we can bring approved models. We’ll need to confirm which are acceptable from your side.

[11:09] Maya Patel: One thing: we can’t just pull random containers from the internet. Everything needs to be from approved registries and scanned.

[11:18] Simran Kaur: Yep, that’s common. We can support private registry flows.

[11:22] Avery Johnson: Chris, any other security gating items? SAML, RBAC, IP allowlisting.

[11:28] Chris Reynolds: SAML is required. RBAC. Audit trail for admin actions. Also we need to know how you handle incident response and who has access to the environment.

[11:39] Avery Johnson: Understood. Our Private option reduces Redwood operator access by design, but we’ll document it.

[11:47] Simran Kaur: On the benchmarking you mentioned, Elena—how do you want to measure? Traffic replay, synthetic prompts, etc.

[11:54] Elena Torres: We can do traffic replay from logs, but again, PHI. We can create a representative synthetic set, but we need it to be realistic. We also have some de-identified notes.

[12:08] Simran Kaur: Okay. We can propose a plan: define prompt sets, measure p50/p95, tokens per second, and error rates. Also cost per request.

[12:19] Avery Johnson: For timeline, when are you hoping to decide?

[12:23] Maya Patel: If we can start a pilot in June, we’d like to decide by end of June, early July. But security review can take… a while.

[12:34] Chris Reynolds: Minimum 4 weeks if it’s a new vendor, unless we can reuse prior assessments.

[12:40] Avery Johnson: Got it. So earlier we can start the security diligence, the better.

[12:45] Simran Kaur: Can you describe your current audit log requirements more concretely? Like what fields are required.

[12:52] Chris Reynolds: Request ID, timestamp, principal, action, result, source IP, and any admin changes. For inference calls, we want model version, region, and token counts, but no prompts.

[13:06] Simran Kaur: Okay. And do you need tenant separation? Like multiple internal teams.

[13:11] Maya Patel: Yes. We’re multi-tenant internally. We need separate API keys and quotas by product group.

[13:18] Avery Johnson: That maps to how a lot of customers use us. Dedicated projects or per-route configs.

[13:24] Elena Torres: Another issue: when we tested vLLM, we struggled to do rollouts. Like model versioning. We had downtime.

[13:31] Simran Kaur: Yeah, rollouts are tricky. Redwood has model version pinning and canary policies. For Private we’d set that up via config.

[13:42] Maya Patel: Can you do automatic fallback? Like if a model is unhealthy, route to a backup.

[13:47] Simran Kaur: Yes, via routing policies. But we’d need to define which backup is acceptable because for regulated workloads you may not want silent changes. We can make it explicit.

[13:59] Chris Reynolds: Right, we don’t want “surprise model changes.”

[14:03] Avery Johnson: Totally. It can be controlled.

[14:06] Elena Torres: We do want reliability. We’ve seen vendor APIs just throttle us with 429s.

[14:12] Avery Johnson: Yep. In dedicated/private you can get more predictable throughput.

[14:18] Simran Kaur: Can you share what your error budget is? Like acceptable error rates.

[14:23] Elena Torres: For clinician workflow, basically it has to work. Maybe 99.9% success per request. For triage, maybe a little lower but still high.

[14:35] Simran Kaur: Okay.

[14:37] Avery Johnson: I want to be mindful of time. Maybe we do a quick recap and then lock next steps.

[14:43] Maya Patel: Sure.

[14:45] Avery Johnson: What I heard: you have PHI-adjacent workloads, need VPC/private connectivity, no content retention, audit logs export, SAML/RBAC, US-only. You’re currently mixing vendor APIs and early self-hosted vLLM, seeing unstable p95 and ops pain. Success is stable latency, predictable cost, and passing security review without exceptions. That accurate?

[15:08] Maya Patel: Yes.

[15:09] Chris Reynolds: Yep.

[15:10] Elena Torres: That’s right.

[15:12] Simran Kaur: I’ll add: we need to align on a pilot plan—workload, traffic shape, and metrics. We’ll send a checklist of what we need.

[15:21] Avery Johnson: Great. Before we jump, any immediate “hard stop” questions? Like, if we can’t do X, you’re done.

[15:28] Chris Reynolds: The big one is prompt/response retention. If you can’t guarantee no retention, it’s a no.

[15:34] Simran Kaur: Understood.

[15:35] Maya Patel: And private network path.

[15:38] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[15:40] Simran Kaur: One clarifying question: do you require that the inference compute is in your account, or can it be managed by Redwood in a customer-dedicated VPC?

[15:50] Maya Patel: Ideally in our account, but we can evaluate. The important part is network isolation and access control.

[15:58] Chris Reynolds: And contractual terms, BAA.

[16:02] Avery Johnson: Okay. We can provide options.

[16:05] (Brief crosstalk)

[16:06] Elena Torres: Also, performance. We care about first token latency. Some systems are fast overall but slow to start.

[16:13] Simran Kaur: Yep. We measure TTFT separately. We can tune batching for that.

[16:18] Avery Johnson: Cool. Next steps I propose: (1) we send security packet and private deployment overview, (2) schedule technical deep dive with Simran, Chris, maybe one of your network folks, and (3) in parallel, Elena shares whatever baseline metrics you have and a representative prompt set approach.

[16:37] Maya Patel: Works.

[16:38] Chris Reynolds: Fine.

[16:39] Elena Torres: Yes.

[16:41] Avery Johnson: Great. One last thing: for design partner, it can be purely private—no public case study—at least initially. But we may later ask for a reference call or anonymized write-up if it goes well.

[16:53] Maya Patel: That’s reasonable.

[16:55] Avery Johnson: Alright. I’ll follow up with an email and times. Thanks everyone.

[17:01] Simran Kaur: Thanks.

[17:02] Chris Reynolds: Thanks.

[17:03] Elena Torres: Thank you.

[17:04] Maya Patel: Bye.

(Note: Fireflies transcript ended early due to recording stop; remaining ~30 minutes of the meeting continued with similar discussion around network topology, logging boundaries, and procurement timelines.)
